extraction.name: MMMU: Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning
extraction.description: A benchmark of 11,550 college-level multimodal questions designed to evaluate expert-level perception, subject knowledge, and reasoning in multimodal foundation models. It covers six disciplines, 30 subjects, 183 subfields, and 30 image types, with interleaved text and images. It includes 10,861 multiple-choice questions and 689 open-ended questions.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue; Yuansheng Ni; Kai Zhang; Tianyu Zheng; Ruoqi Liu; Ge Zhang; Samuel Stevens; Dongfu Jiang; Weiming Ren; Yuxuan Sun; Cong Wei; Botao Yu; Ruibin Yuan; Renliang Sun; Ming Yin; Boyuan Zheng; Zhenzhu Yang; Yibo Liu; Wenhao Huang; Huan Sun; Yu Su; Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: Xiang Yue et al. MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv:2311.16502v4, 13 June 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors first selected university subjects in which visual inputs commonly provide valuable information, resulting in 30 subjects across six disciplines. Over 50 university students, including coauthors and specialists in the selected majors, manually collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources, creating new questions using their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to use diverse sources, respect copyright and licensing restrictions, avoid sources prohibiting copying or redistribution, and prefer questions whose answers were not immediately accessible. Approximately 13,000 questions were initially collected and subsequently cleaned and filtered to produce 11,550 questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Explanations were annotated only when available. The final benchmark contains explanations for 2,035 questions, representing 17.62% of the questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: College exams, quizzes, textbooks, lecture materials, free online resources, and other study materials. Some questions were newly created by annotators using their subject expertise.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Authors corrected formatting deviations and typographical errors, standardized question formats, removed confirmed duplicates, and excluded approximately 10% of the initially collected problems classified as very easy.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which authors reviewed and removed when confirmed. Problems were distributed among coauthors for standardized-format and typo checking. Authors assigned difficulty levels of very easy, easy, medium, or hard; very easy problems that did not meet the benchmark's design criteria were excluded. Each sample was stored in a separate JSON file named subject_{Number}.json, with images named image_{QuesNum}_{ImageNum}.png and referenced by file paths within questions, options, or explanations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: University students specializing in the relevant subjects manually collected and annotated questions. Guidelines required English, college-level, unambiguous questions containing one or more images and answerable through a single correct option or a short answer. Annotators recorded question type, question text, answer options for multiple-choice questions, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation when available. Long-answer questions were to be avoided. Authors categorized difficulty levels, and a secondary review team vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Annotators were instructed to respect source copyright and licensing rules and avoid questions containing private information.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A custom web interface for data annotation and verification developed by Tianyu Zheng.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Ambiguous or unclear instances were to be flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized annotation approach. A secondary review team vetted annotation quality and guideline adherence. In the analysis of 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances, 2% were attributed to annotation errors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including coauthors, specializing in the selected university majors and representing various disciplines and subjects.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The annotation protocol specifies regular audits of random dataset samples to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Xiang Yue led the dataset release. A live-updating model leaderboard is available at https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to help monitor progress toward Expert AGI. The paper discusses Expert AGI as potentially reaching a substitution threshold for human labor in many industries, with significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption, making progress monitoring societally important.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors acknowledge that manual curation may carry biases. Subject selection favors fields in which visual inputs are commonly used; law and linguistics were excluded because sufficient relevant multimodal problems were difficult to find.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI: there is no direct mapping between benchmark performance and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, and college examinations do not encompass all tasks an AGI should tackle. Its college-level focus and manually curated content limit its comprehensiveness and may introduce biases. Annotation inaccuracies were identified in the sampled model-error analysis.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of multimodal foundation models on expert-level perception, subject knowledge, and reasoning, and monitoring progress toward Expert AGI. The dataset contains a 150-question few-shot development set with five questions per subject, a 900-question validation set for hyperparameter selection and prompt engineering, and a 10,500-question test set. Development examples are used for in-context learning experiments. The main experiments use zero-shot evaluation without fine-tuning or few-shot demonstrations. Evaluation uses micro-averaged accuracy and rule-based answer matching for multiple-choice and concise open-ended responses.
